title: Reading James and 1 Peter

objectives.can: Read the imperatival, proverbial Greek of James and the more periodic Greek of 1 Peter.

explanation.summary: James and 1 Peter are both letters in good Greek, but they sound different. James speaks in short commands and sayings, often with images. 1 Peter builds long sentences from participles and relative clauses. This lesson describes both and sends you into the long opening sentences of 1 Peter.

sections.heading: James: command after command
body: James uses imperatives constantly, and it is a good letter in which to practise them. Many are second person, like Πᾶσαν χαρὰν ἡγήσασθε in James 1:2, an aorist imperative: 'consider it all joy'. Many more are third person: ἐχέτω in 1:4, αἰτείτω in 1:5, Καυχάσθω in 1:9, λεγέτω in 1:13. The third-person imperative is translated 'let him …' or 'let it …': ἡ δὲ ὑπομονὴ ἔργον τέλειον ἐχέτω, 'let endurance have its perfect work'.

The commands are often attached to a condition or a time: ὅταν with an aorist subjunctive in 1:2, 'whenever you fall into', and εἰ δέ τις … λείπεται in 1:5, 'but if anyone lacks'. The condition sets the circumstance, and the imperative gives what to do.

sections.heading: James: sayings and images
body: The letter is full of short, proverb-like sayings and comparisons. Readers often compare it with Old Testament wisdom writing. In 1:6 the one who doubts is compared to the sea: ἔοικεν κλύδωνι θαλάσσης. In 1:10–11 the rich person is compared to the flower of grass, and οὕτως in 1:11 brings the comparison round to the rich person: οὕτως καὶ ὁ πλούσιος … μαρανθήσεται.

Notice the verbs of the image in 1:11: ἀνέτειλεν, ἐξήρανεν, ἐξέπεσεν, ἀπώλετο are all aorists. Grammarians often read such aorists as stating what regularly happens (a 'gnomic' use) and not as a report of one particular event. Read them as a vivid description of the whole process, and notice that the last verb, μαρανθήσεται, is a future about the rich person.

sections.heading: 1 Peter: long sentences from participles
body: 1 Peter is the other style. In this edition 1:3–5 is one very long sentence, and 1:6–9 is a second, joined to it by the relative ἐν ᾧ (some editors punctuate the passage differently, as a single sentence). The first starts without a finite verb: Εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεός, 'blessed be God' (the verb is understood). It then runs on by attaching phrase after phrase.

Two devices carry it. The first is the participle with the article, such as ὁ … ἀναγεννήσας in 1:3, which attaches a description of God. The second is the participle in agreement with 'you', which adds one circumstance after another: τετηρημένην in 1:4, which agrees with κληρονομίαν; φρουρουμένους in 1:5, which agrees with ὑμᾶς at the end of 1:4; λυπηθέντες in 1:6; ἰδόντες, ὁρῶντες and πιστεύοντες in 1:8; κομιζόμενοι in 1:9. When you meet a participle, find the word it agrees with in gender, number and case, and it will tell you what is being described.

sections.heading: 1 Peter: relatives that link the sentence
body: The other device is the relative pronoun at the start of a clause, which both points back and starts a new clause. 1:6 begins ἐν ᾧ, 1:8 begins ὃν οὐκ ἰδόντες ἀγαπᾶτε, and 1:10 begins Περὶ ἧς σωτηρίας. In each, the relative takes its gender and number from the thing it points back to and its case from its own clause. These relatives are the hinges: they connect new matter to what came before.

A reading tip: when you reach a long sentence in 1 Peter, first mark the finite verbs (there are few), then mark the relatives, then attach the participles and the prepositional phrases. ἵνα in 1:7 starts a purpose clause: ἵνα τὸ δοκίμιον ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως … εὑρεθῇ, with a subjunctive passive.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read 1 Peter 1:3–12 first for its shape: a blessing of God (1:3), a hope laid up (1:4–5), joy in trial (1:6–7), love for one not seen (1:8–9), and the prophets who searched for this salvation (1:10–12). Then read again with the grammar: find the verbs, note the relatives, and match each participle to the word it describes. The questions for this lesson come from both letters, so that you can hear the difference.

misunderstandings: Reading a third-person imperative such as αἰτείτω as an indicative ('he asks'). The ending -τω marks it as a command: 'let him ask'.
Treating the aorists of James 1:11 as a report of a single past day. They describe a regular pattern, as the image of the flower requires.
Looking for a finite verb in 1 Peter 1:3 and finding none. The blessing is a verbless exclamation, and the sentence continues from there.
Linking a participle in 1 Peter to the nearest noun without checking its gender, number and case.

deeper.heading: Two good Greek styles
body: Commentators have often noted that James and 1 Peter are among the better-written parts of the New Testament and that they differ from each other. How the letters came to be written in this Greek, and how far their authors relied on help, are questions argued by scholars. The grammar only shows that one letter is built from commands and images, and the other from long, linked periods.

check.prompt: What does ὁ γὰρ διακρινόμενος ἔοικεν κλύδωνι θαλάσσης (words 6–11) say?

quoted.title: James
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: For the sea wavers like a person
For the one who wavers is like a surge of the sea
For the one who wavers will rule the sea
For no one wavers on the sea
check.explain: ὁ διακρινόμενος is an article with a present participle, 'the one who wavers'. ἔοικεν takes the dative κλύδωνι, 'is like a surge', and θαλάσσης is genitive, 'of the sea'. γάρ gives the reason for the command to ask without wavering.

check.prompt: What is the subject of λεγέτω (word 2), and what is it?

quoted.title: James
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: There is no subject; it is an infinitive
μηδείς, with a third-person imperative: 'let no one say'
πειραζόμενος, with an indicative: 'the tempted one says'
θεός, with an imperative: 'let God say'
check.explain: μηδεὶς πειραζόμενος is the subject phrase, 'no one being tempted'. λεγέτω has the third-person imperative ending -τω, and the negative μή-word goes with it.

check.explain: ὅς is masculine singular nominative, agreeing with ἀνήρ, and it is the subject of ὑπομένει. πειρασμόν is the object of that verb.

options: The application of the image to the rich person: so also the rich will fade away
A new image about the sun
check.explain: οὕτως means 'in this way'. It ends the picture of the sun and the grass and applies it to ὁ πλούσιος, whose fate is stated by the future μαρανθήσεται.

check.prompt: With which word does τετηρημένην (word 7) agree?

options: κληρονομίαν (word 1): the inheritance, kept in heaven
check.explain: τετηρημένην is perfect passive participle, accusative singular feminine, like κληρονομίαν. It tells what has been done to the inheritance: it has been kept.

check.prompt: Which word does τοὺς … φρουρουμένους (words 0, 4) describe?

options: ὑμᾶς, at the end of the previous verse: you who are guarded
Nothing; it is a finite verb
check.explain: φρουρουμένους is a present passive participle, accusative plural masculine, and with the article τούς it describes εἰς ὑμᾶς of 1:4. θεοῦ is genitive singular, σωτηρίαν is singular feminine.

check.prompt: What does ὃν οὐκ ἰδόντες ἀγαπᾶτε (words 0–3) say?

quoted.title: 1 Peter
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: Whom you love although you have not seen him
Who does not love those who see
Whom you did not see and will not love
check.explain: ὅν is the relative, object of both the participle and the verb. οὐκ ἰδόντες is an aorist participle with the sense 'though you have not seen'; ἀγαπᾶτε is the main verb, second person plural.

check.prompt: What is the subject of εὑρεθῇ (word 14)?

quoted.title: 1 Peter
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: τὸ δοκίμιον ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως: the testing of your faith
check.explain: τὸ δοκίμιον is neuter singular nominative and takes εὑρεθῇ, an aorist passive subjunctive after ἵνα. χρυσίου is genitive and is what the testing is compared to: πολυτιμότερον χρυσίου, 'more precious than gold'.

reading.why: Ten verses that carry one long argument by participles and relative pronouns (ἐν ᾧ, ὃν, περὶ ἧς), beginning with a verbless blessing and moving through trials and hope to the prophets.
